summary: An informational memo from the Internet architecture community that makes two recommendations to improve Internet performance: test and widely deploy active queue management in routers, and keep working on better end-to-end congestion control. It was replaced by RFC 7567.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router's queue fills up, the usual rule is to throw away whatever arrives next. That makes queues stay full, so everything waits longer than it needs to, and a burst of traffic loses many packets at once. The RFC recommends a different rule: drop a packet early, and drop it at random, so that senders slow down gently and the queue has room left for the next burst.

subtitle: Why routers should drop packets early and at random instead of waiting for the queue to fill.

tldr.problem: TCP's congestion avoidance in the hosts was not enough to keep the Internet healthy. Routers filled their queues and then dropped whatever arrived next, which penalised delay, wasted bandwidth and could let one connection take all the queue space.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends that routers implement active queue management, in which packets are dropped before the buffer is full. The recommended algorithm is Random Early Detection, which drops packets with a probability that rises as the estimated average queue size grows, between two thresholds.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2309 is an Informational document from April 1998 and has been obsoleted by RFC 7567, which records the current state of active queue management.

today: RFC 2309 is an Informational document from April 1998, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7567, which records the current state of active queue management. The RFC itself says it provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and that the discussion applies to best-effort traffic.

sections.title: The Problem: Congestion Collapse
sections.content:
The Internet is built on a connectionless packet service, and that design has been shown to work well. But the advantages are not without cost: careful design is needed to give good service under heavy load. A lack of attention to the dynamics of packet forwarding can produce severe service degradation, or what the RFC calls an Internet meltdown. The phenomenon was first observed during the early growth of the Internet in the mid 1980s, and is technically called congestion collapse.

The original fix came from Van Jacobson, who developed from 1986 the congestion avoidance mechanisms that TCP implementations are now required to have. They operate in the hosts and cause TCP connections to back off during congestion, so TCP flows are said to be responsive to congestion signals from the network. It is mainly these algorithms that prevent collapse today.

But research since 1988 showed that they are not sufficient in all circumstances, because there is a limit to how much control can be exerted from the edges of the network. Some mechanisms are needed in the routers to complement the endpoint algorithms. The RFC separates two classes of router algorithm: queue management, which manages the length of packet queues by dropping packets when necessary, and scheduling, which decides which packet to send next and so allocates bandwidth among flows. The two are closely related but address different performance problems, and this memo is about the first of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts already slow down when the network drops their packets, and that has kept the Internet working. But the hosts can only do so much, and the routers themselves need to help by managing their queues sensibly.

sections.title: Why Active Queue Management
sections.content:
The traditional way to manage a router queue is to give it a maximum length in packets, accept packets until that length is reached, and then reject incoming packets until the queue drains. This is called tail drop, because the packet that arrived most recently is the one dropped when the queue is full. It has served the Internet well, but it has two important drawbacks.

The first is lock-out. In some situations tail drop lets a single connection, or a few flows, take all the queue space and keep the others out. The RFC attributes this to synchronisation and other timing effects. The second is full queues. Tail drop signals congestion only when the queue has become full, so queues stay full or nearly full for long periods.

The RFC is careful about the trade-off this appears to involve. It looks like a choice between low delay and high throughput, but it is not, because packet bursts matter. Even though TCP limits the size of a flow's window, packets often arrive at routers in bursts. If the queue is full, an arriving burst causes several packets to be dropped, which can cause many flows to back off together, followed by a period of low link use and reduced throughput. The purpose of buffering is to absorb bursts and send them during the quiet that follows. So keeping queues normally small can raise throughput as well as lower delay, and queue limits should reflect the size of the bursts that need absorbing rather than the steady-state queue size.

Two other disciplines can be applied once the queue is full: random drop on full, which drops a randomly selected packet from the queue, and drop front on full, which drops the packet at the front. Both solve lock-out, but neither solves full queues.

The solution for responsive flows is for routers to drop packets before the queue becomes full, so that senders can respond before the buffers overflow. That proactive approach is active queue management, and it gives the router control over when and how many packets to drop.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things go wrong with the ordinary rule. One connection can take all the room and starve the others, and the queue stays full, which means everything waits. Dropping early fixes both: there is usually space free, and senders get told to slow down before the buffer overflows.

sections.title: Random Early Detection
sections.content:
Random Early Detection, or RED, is an active queue management algorithm for routers. Unlike traditional algorithms that drop packets only when the buffer is full, RED drops arriving packets probabilistically, with the probability of a drop rising as the estimated average queue size grows. RED responds to a time-averaged queue length rather than an instantaneous one, so a queue that has been mostly empty in the recent past will not see drops, while a queue that has recently been relatively full will drop newly arriving packets more often.

RED has two main parts. The first is estimating the average queue size, either in the forwarding path using a simple exponentially weighted moving average, or in the background using a similar mechanism. The queue size may be measured in packets or in bytes. When the average is computed in the forwarding path there is a special case: if a packet arrives and the queue is empty, the computation has to take into account how much time has passed since the queue went empty.

The second part is the drop decision. Two parameters matter most. minth is the average queue size below which no packets are dropped, and maxth is the average queue size above which all packets are dropped. Between the two thresholds the drop probability rises linearly from 0 to maxp. A naive implementation would compute a new random number at each packet arrival and compare it with that probability; the more efficient method described in the RED paper computes a random number once for each dropped packet. The decision can be made in packet mode, ignoring packet sizes, or in byte mode, taking the size of the incoming packet into account.

RED controls the average queue size while still absorbing bursts without loss, and its use of randomness breaks up the synchronised processes that lead to lock-out. The RFC reports that all the available empirical evidence shows that deploying active queue management would bring substantial performance benefits, with seemingly no disadvantages, and that RED should be widely deployed. It notes one extreme case where RED is not a cure, though it may still help: a very large number of flows, each so tiny that its fair share would be less than a single packet per round-trip time.
sections.plainLanguage: RED watches the average length of the queue rather than the length at this instant. Below the low threshold nothing is dropped. Above the high threshold everything is dropped. In between, packets are dropped at random with a probability that rises with the queue length, so senders slow down a little at a time rather than all at once.

sections.title: Managing Aggressive Flows
sections.content:
The success of the Internet depends on the congestion avoidance mechanisms in TCP. Because TCP backs off during congestion, many connections can share a congested link with bandwidth shared reasonably equitably. That works because all flows run basically the same algorithms, conformant with the TCP specification.

The RFC introduces the term TCP-compatible for a flow that behaves under congestion like one produced by a conformant TCP: it is responsive to congestion notification, and in steady state it uses no more bandwidth than a conformant TCP under comparable conditions of drop rate, round-trip time and maximum transmission unit. Flows fall into three classes: TCP-compatible, unresponsive, meaning they do not slow down when congestion occurs, and responsive but not TCP-compatible.

The last two classes hold the aggressive flows that threaten Internet performance. The first threat is from unresponsive flows. There is a growing set of UDP applications whose congestion avoidance is inadequate or absent, such as packet voice and video and multicast bulk transport. Left alone, these could cause a new congestion collapse. The RFC says all UDP streaming applications should incorporate effective congestion avoidance, but also that the network must be able to protect itself against unresponsive flows, and that deploying such mechanisms would give every streaming application an incentive to become responsive.

The second threat is from transport implementations that respond to congestion notification but are deliberately or accidentally not TCP-compatible. A vendor could offer a faster TCP by being more aggressive with bandwidth. The logical consequence is a spiral of ever more aggressive implementations, ending with no effective congestion avoidance and a chronically congested Internet. The RFC notes that the same effect can be had without changing TCP at all, by opening multiple connections to the same place, as some web browsers have done.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP's fairness depends on everybody playing by the same rules. Traffic that ignores congestion signals, or that backs off less than TCP does, takes more than its share. The RFC says both groups are a growing threat and calls for research and measurement to find router mechanisms that can handle them.

sections.title: The Two Recommendations
sections.content:
The first recommendation is that Internet routers should implement some active queue management mechanism, to manage queue lengths, reduce end-to-end latency, reduce packet dropping and avoid lock-out. The default mechanism for FIFO queues is Random Early Detection, and unless a developer has reasons to provide another equivalent mechanism, RED is recommended.

The second recommendation is that it is urgent to begin or continue research, engineering and measurement work on mechanisms to deal with flows that are unresponsive to congestion notification, or that are responsive but more aggressive than TCP.

The RFC warns that wide deployment of RED will expose engineering issues, such as implementation questions for Gigabit routers, the use of RED in layer 2 switches, and the possible use of extra considerations such as priority when deciding which packets to drop. It also stresses that deploying RED will not by itself achieve the goals of the second recommendation.

Deployment of RED is described as enabling other new functionality. One example is the addition of explicit congestion notification to the Internet architecture, as a congestion signal in addition to packet drops. A second is queues with packets of different drop priorities, where packets are still transmitted in the order they arrived, but during congestion the ones with lower drop priority are discarded first.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo ends with two asks of the community: put active queue management in routers, and start working out how to deal with traffic that does not behave like TCP. It also points out that the first change would make it possible to add explicit congestion notification and priority-based dropping.

items.label: Minimum threshold
items.desc: The average queue size below which no packets are dropped.

items.label: Maximum threshold
items.desc: The average queue size above which all packets are dropped.

items.label: Maximum probability
items.desc: As the average queue size varies from minth to maxth, packets are dropped with a probability that varies linearly from 0 to maxp.

items.label: Average queue size
items.desc: An exponentially weighted moving average, computed either in the forwarding path or in the background. RED responds to this average and not to the instantaneous queue length.

viz.caption: WHAT ACTIVE QUEUE MANAGEMENT IS SUPPOSED TO BUY (RFC 2309)

items.title: Fewer packets dropped
items.text: Keeping the average queue small leaves buffer space free to absorb bursts, so a burst does not cause a cascade of drops.

items.title: Lower delay
items.text: Small queues mean less waiting, which matters most for interactive work such as short web transfers and voice and video sessions.

items.title: No lock-out
items.text: Because there is almost always buffer available for an incoming packet, one flow cannot take the whole queue and starve the others.

items.title: Room for bursts
items.text: The purpose of buffering is to absorb packets that arrive in bursts and send them during the quiet that follows.
